column4: comment

Ethan Harris stated he lives in the Hillcrest historic neighborhood with his family. He stated that since living in the area, the mall continues to buy up property and intrude into the neighborhood. He expressed his concern with the proposed Wright Development property, saying the neighboring street will become overflow parking for the apartments, and said this would bring more crime and traffic to the area. He then stated the council has received a nine-page petition to halt the development.

Jared Moore expressed how he feels the residents in the area would not be listened to, but expressed thanks to certain members of the council for voting to pass the moratorium. He asked the council to reconsider what could be built on the property, saying the attempted bank development on the property a few years back would have been a great addition to the community.

Stephanie Visnaw stated that giving unlimited height maximums and high density housing the ability to be built next to residential zones is a bad idea. She expressed that high density housing projects cause parking issues for surrounding neighborhoods. She then read a few Facebook comments on the Orem Police Department’s page expressing concern with parking issues caused by high density housing developments.

Byron Taylor expressed his concern with “communication deficiencies” in Orem City. He stated that he received a flyer in the mail informing him about a planning commission meeting that was taking place later that day. He expressed this was received much too late for him to attend the meeting. Mr. Taylor then stated he wanted to find some planning information and had to jump through way too many hoops to get it.

Richard Davis stated he and Sam Lentz were the instigators of this petition. He expressed he has had past experience being part of a group facing prejudice and stated was grateful when someone stood up for his group. He stated that by including marginalized groups in things like library displays can teach understanding and bring the community together.

John Livingston stated he works with an organization called Now I Can that helps treat children with Neurological disorders. He stated the nonprofit organization would like to buy some property in Orem to build a treatment center. He asked the council for support on this project.

Neal Lebaron stated he is a board member for Now I Can. He stated a former Vice President of the United States said the moral test of any government is how they treat children, elders, and the sick. He then expressed that he would like the council to show consideration for the group.
Patty Henwood stated she would like to see the concerned property acquired by the Now I Can nonprofit organization and asked the council to help with this.

Stephanie Visnaw thanked the City Council for continuing to make changes to the State Street Districts. She has heard from several residents that developers and commercial property owners have taken some liberties and are not being held accountable for all city ordinances. She feels larger developers are controlling the meetings and are given preferential treatment and

Lory Towman stated there are multiple houses getting damaged in a residential area near Geneva road and Sleepy Ridge Golf Course. She stated parts of houses are shifting and cracking, causing unsightly and unsafe living conditions for residents. She said this could be caused by removing and pumping ground water out of the area, and asked the council to look into the problem.

Carol Miles stated she has lived near the Sienna Villas project area for 35 years. She said that if Sienna Villas is allowed to expand, it will bring unwanted traffic and parking issues into the area. Ms. Miles stated the street she lives on is a very tight-knit community, and she would like to see it stay that way. She then asked the City Council to not rezone the two family lots to a zone that high-density could be built on.

Stephanie Visnaw expressed that Orem rezoning family lots near the Sienna Villas to make room for more apartment units would be intruding on residential neighborhoods and would not be responsible growth.

James Patterson stated he lives on Terrace Drive which is right next to the Sienna Villas project and stated that adding additional units to the project will add problematic traffic and parking to the area

Henry Miles stated he lives on Terrace Drive, right by the Sienna Villas project. He expressed his concern that project plans keep changing and adding more units will negatively impact traffic and parking in the area. He asked the city council to not rezone the area.

Linsey Studebaker stated there is a mental healthcare business run near her home. She stated there is a man who is in care at that facility who keeps getting out of the facility and causing issues. She stated the workers at the business cannot control him. She asked the council to take action to move the business out of the neighborhood.
Jack Bingham stated he lives in the Sienna Villas area. He stated the area is not fit for more high- density housing, and that traffic and parking would be negatively impacted.

LaNae Millet stated the proposed addition to Sienna Villas would be too close to existing homes and would add traffic and parking issues to the area. She asked the council to “stop the creep” of high density into neighborhoods.

Ken Hone stated Orem has too much high-density housing and some surrounding cities are not holding their fair share of the burden. He asked the council to be wise about how they handle the growth of Orem.
Mara Garcia expressed her concerns with expanding high-density housing near Terrace drive.
Mike Christensen read a poem commemorating the 400th anniversary of Thanksgiving.
Murray Low expressed his thanks to Mayor Brunst and Mr. Sumner for their service to the city and stated they will be missed.

John Barrick thanked the council for making the changes to the City Planning Commission appointment and approval process and hiring legal counsel. Mr. Barrick then stated he supports the removal of the proposed Planning Commission members.

Jonni-Sue Schilaty expressed her support for Mayor Young and for passed ordinances and resolutions regarding the Planning Commission appointment process and the City Council Legal Counsel. Mrs. Schilaty then expressed her distaste for the UTA system in Orem and said she would not like to see it expand.

Barry Roberts expressed he found it strange that the Mayor and Council considers the Planning Commission a legislative body. He stated the planning commission has no legislative, and only administrative power. Mr. Roberts then also expressed his concern for the hired legislative council.

Heidi Cox read a statement from Marisa Bentley, which expressed how she is saddened the Mayor and Council want to remove her from the Planning Commission. She stated she would like to finish her terms along with the other members up for removal.

Marcia Reinhart stated she lives in a neighborhood where streetlights were recently updated, but the work still hasn't been finished, and the lights aren't on. She asked the council how they were going to start large new projects when they can't finish current small ones.

Cissy Rasmussen expressed her concern with the Ordinance passed during the last council meeting regarding the appointment process of Planning Commission Members. She asked the council not to remove the proposed Planning Commission members. She expressed how she felt the Mayor and Council are not being transparent with the residents, and are giving people who they know and have similar views on issues preferential treatment. Ms. Rasmussen concluded by asking the City Council to embrace change in the city.

David Moulton stated he has been an Orem resident for 25 years and was a former member and chair of the Planning Commission. Mr. Moulton then expressed how he does not agree with the changes the Council has made to the Planning Commission, stating they have made a political body out of something that has been a volunteer citizen commission in the past. He then asked them not to remove the proposed members.

Haysam Sakar expressed his support for the new Mayor and Council and stated he is in support of the Legal Counsel hired by the Council. Mr. Sakar then expressed his support for the removal of Mickey Cochran from the Planning Commission.

Carl Cook stated he has never seen Planning Commission members be removed like this and stated the Mayor and Council are making the Planning Commission a political and legislative body when they are not meant to be. He asked the Council to not remove the proposed members.

Jenn Young expressed her concern for the direction the city has been heading in for the last few years. She asked the Council to help Orem stay affordable. She also expressed her support for removing the proposed Planning Commission members.

Quin Mecham asked the council to value diverse and politically independent citizen commissions and stated the best leaders always receive advise from a wide range of people who's opinions differ from theirs. Mr. Mecham then asked the Council to focus on transparency and expressed how he felt the processes leading up to tonight removal vote have not been transparent and asked the Council to not remove the members.

Eleni Wilding stated how she wants the Planning Commission to be held accountable to the citizens and asked how this would be done if they were not held accountable to the City Council. Ms. Wilding then stated a recent article in the Daily Herald could be considered 'Fake News' and that Mickey Cochran did call residents statistically insignificant. She concluded by thanking the Council for taking the bold action they have by changing Planning Commission structure.

Mike Preston stated he attended a school board meeting last year where parents were locked out. He expressed how he feels this action was illegal, and should not have been done. Mr. Preston then went on to explain how he felt the Alpine School Board has become too powerful and asked the Council to support splitting off from the Alpine School District and to also include Lindon in this action.
Sicilia Palmer expressed her support for the idea of splitting from the Alpine School District and asked the Council to investigate including Lindon and Pleasant Grove in the split.

John Barrick stated he was in favor of the proposed study looking into splitting off from the Alpine School District. He also explained how he felt property taxes were too high because of Alpine School District and stated they are too large, and have too much power. Mr. Barrick then went on to state how he feels quality of education has gone down in the last few years significantly. As an example, he stated that Northridge Elementary pulled all specialty programs from their school and replaced them with special-needs programing. Mr. Barrick expressed how this is dangerous and scary for the children. Mr. Barrick concluded by stating the Alpine School District has also denied gramma requests and feels they are taking too much tax money from Orem residents.

John Hasan stated he would like to see Orem City have an open softball team, and volunteered to be the coach. He went on to express how he would like this program to be prominent on the Parks and Recreation website.

Cissy Rasmussen stated all of her children go to schools within Alpine School District and expressed how she was opposed to splitting off from them. Mrs. Rasmussen suggested the council should meet with Alpine School District, who have already done many in-depth studies which suggest splitting the district would be negative for Orem City residents.
Quinn Mecham expressed that he was in favor of the proposed Utah Lake resolution and asked the Council to be insistent in asking for part control in any authority that could be a governing

Mike Carpenter expressed how he feels the Alpine School District is declining in quality annually and stated how he feels that staying in the Alpine School District could be detrimental to the future of the city’s children.

Kathy Ambrose expressed how she feels kids in school need to have a full stomach before being able to learn, and that issue should be focused on first before looking at splitting from the Alpine School District.

Jim Hadlock stated he would like to see a uniform water conservation policy between the largest water users within the city and expressed how he hopes to see more Latino police officers. Mr. Hadlock concluded by stating how he feels Orem City should be doing more to help low-income residents and the homeless within our community.

John Barrick thanked the Council for looking into splitting off from the Alpine School District. He then stated the district has been making it difficult for Council Members to attend school meetings and concluded by voicing his concerns with multiple issues with the Alpine School District such as overly-large class sizes and property tax usage.

Scott Swain expressed how he feels because of the Covid-19 pandemic, Orem has lost a certain sense of community, and stated he wants to propose an event at the Scera Shell every Saturday to redevelop community within the city. Mrs. Lauret responded the city holds a summer concert series every Monday night in the City Center Park, and asked if Mr. Swain would be interested in partnering on that. Mr. Swain responded and expressed that he would like to see both events held.

Vanessa Rucker stated how she felt there are multiple issues with the choker islands that were installed on Palisade Drive. She expressed that the choker islands are unsightly, force cyclists into the middle of the road, and are easily hidden by snow. Ms. Rucker concluded by asking the council to remove the choker islands and speed tables from Palisade Drive, and replace them with standard speed bumps.

Cissy Rasmussen encouraged the council to invite questions from, and include teachers and parents in the investigation of splitting off from the Alpine School District. Ms. Rasmussen also asked the council to include more information regarding the potential split on the City's website.

Jenna Hyatt asked the council to not make a decision on the feasibility study before having conversations with parents, teachers, and PTA representatives. She went on to state how declining student numbers could raise taxes on Orem residents because we will rely solely on our own property taxes.

Abby Farrows expressed how residents in the Palisade area were not properly informed on the speed mitigation devices that were being installed in their neighborhood. She then expressed how she feels the survey Palisade area residents received could be bias, and 11 of the 13 questions had to do with pedestrian safety in general, instead of the choker islands specifically.

Benjamin Brooks expressed how he felt the choker islands were placed too close to corners, which could cause cars to hit them accidentally. He also went on to state the choker islands can also force cyclists into the center of the road, creating danger for both them and drivers in the area.

Andrea Driggs stated the choker islands can be hard to see, especially in snowy conditions. She also stated how she felt the choker islands are unsightly and there are too many of them. Ms. Driggs then concluded her statements by expressing her support for the removal of the choker islands.

Dave Johnston expressed that Palisade Drive is one of eight main streets used for north and south travel within Orem, and then questioned why it is the only one of those streets that has a significant number of speedbumps and other traffic calming measures installed.

Cody Hale stated he has lived in Orem since 1984 and also serves on the Orem Arts Council. He then expressed how he founded the Hale Center Theater in Orem and appreciates the city supporting their business over the many years they have been in Orem.

Ben Whealal stated he recently transferred his son out of Orem High School due to a number of concerns he has with the school. These concerns included discrimination and nepotism within sports programs, and an unfair recruiting process. He also stated Orem High and the Alpine School District did not contest his son’s transfer to another school. Because of these reasons, Mr. Whealal stated Orem should “take control of their own destiny” and form their own school district.

John Barrick stated in the past an Orem resident publicly stated to the Council if an Orem exclusive school district were to be formed, taxes would go up as much as 25%, and services would go down. This individual asked via email to the district: “I needed help with some numbers ASAP. What’s the total cost of running Orem schools, if you break it down from state/federal, etc.? I thought it would be good to give the simplest breakdown possible of the financial situation. It might be more effective than just saying, as I usually do, that taxes will go up and services will go down.” Mr. Barrick then expressed how he feels the Council had been lied to. This individual emailed the whole city of Orem, without any information, to sign a petition to fight against the City Council. Mr. Barrick stated “Orem has paid, in the last 10 years, $465,000,000 dollars in property taxes, received $82,000,000 dollars in bond allocations, and had a net contribution to the Alpine School District of $383,000,000 dollars. In the last 18 years, because that’s all the data that is available, Orem has given $550 million dollars to the Alpine School District net. Mr. Barrick concluded his comments by stating though residents can lie to the Council, and lie to the residents in a petition, and form a political movement based on a lie, you cannot make the $550 million dollars go away.

Tauni Merrell stated she lives near Cascade Drive, where constant disturbing of the peace and traffic violations take place. She stated there are many loud, speeding vehicles going up and down Cascade Drive at all hours of the day. She expressed these vehicles are racing each other and not stopping before merging onto 800 East. She then listed other problems in the area such as people yelling and screaming, parties being held in the parking lots at the top of the drive, and nefarious activities taking place at these parties. Ms. Merrell concluded her comments by asking the city install a locked gate at the bottom of Cascade Drive that closes at dusk.

Peter Merrell stated he lives near Cascade Drive. He stated there are many public nuisances which take place on the road and asked the Council to close it from dusk until dawn. Mr. Merrell concluded his comments by asking the Council to install a locking fence, traffic counter, velocity tracker, decibel monitor, and video surveillance cameras in the area.

Mike Faragher stated that with Orem being “Family City USA,” we should do more to celebrate the children in the community. He then proposed that Orem City should formally recognize children with a city holiday the same way we do for mothers and fathers.
Kary Richardson stated he lives near Cascade Drive and feels speeding, parties in the parking lots, and loud racing are big problems in the area. He asked the Council to act on this.
Terresa Horn stated she lives on Cascade Drive and said she has heard gunshots in the area. She then asked the Council to address the problem.

Jennifer Young stated she has lived in both Davis County and Orem over the past few years and has four kids who have attended both Orem schools and Davis County schools. She stated she is a second-grade teacher and has had her degree for about nine years. Through teaching she has witnessed students come in and out of different schools. Her biggest concern through studying and Facebook observation is that people are making decisions without getting the data first. She is hoping that others can stay open minding and that the data will shed some new light. Mrs. Young concluded she worked at a private school in Davis County where she studied many different school models and believes that local control can be best represented by a smaller number.

Lanae Larson stated she has five children from the ages 17-6 years of age and was anticipating things to eventually go back to normal in the public education system. She ended up pulling her second grader out of public school because she felt as though she couldn’t let him go back to school with the influence that it was having on him. She stated her three older children are still in public schools. She expressed that her children are on a laptop 80% of the time and she believes that there is a push back to get every kid on a laptop because education can be manipulated and distorted. She does not feel that teachers, principals, and parents can keep up with the technology because it is changing so rapidly. Her son who she pulled out of public school now goes to a charter school and one thing she really likes about this is the smaller classroom sizes and more parental involvement. She stated that although her son’s charter school does not have a lot of money, they hold fundraisers and use parental involvement to their advantage. Ms. Larson concluded that she feels by funneling money back into smaller classroom sizes and teachers it will help because she is more concerned with the structure of her child’s mind versus building safety for earthquakes.

Keith Wilson stated he is married to Ada Wilson who has represented Orem and Vineyard for the past four years on the Alpine School Board and is part of a group called Orem and ASD stronger together. Keith feels this issue is not all about money, it’s all about education but education cannot happen without the funding. He feels it has been demonstrated with verifiable historical facts that if Orem becomes its own district and if the schools continue to be funded at current levels, there will be a revenue shortfall of over $21 million dollars requiring a property tax increase. He stated that in the council meeting he attended in April, Mayor Young assured everyone that raising taxes was not the intent and he would not propose a new district that he believed would require a tax increase. He stated an important expectation is any proposed school district would continue to fund schools at the current level and we’re not cutting school funding by tens of millions in order to dodge a tax question. He asked the council on behalf of Orem residents and on behalf of their children that they have assurances that the proposals for a new district will continue to fund schools at the current level. Mr. Wilson concluded that the $21 million dollar figure is not accurate or complete, there are a number of factors that are not included which include, startup costs in the district, interest rates, and inflation and hoped the feasibility study had taken those into account.

Jana Hyatt addressed the Council by stating as a representative democracy they elect them to educate themselves on the issues and so this decision they are going to make tonight whether to put this on the ballot or not will represent their best thinking, their best ability to reason; so let it be no mistake, they are also on the ballot tonight. She continued by indicating the citizens of Orem are going to remember this event and this night. She stated after the feasibility study was presented, she felt their facts showed that it will be more expensive and what they did not tell is how much more expensive it will be. She felt in the study they were very careful to work around very important details and facts so that reading the study doesn’t allow you to see how much it will actually cost. She recommended this issue not go on the ballot because there are better options available, like including other cities. She indicated she recently had a great conversation with someone in the Murray School District, a one city school district, and they can’t rebuild their schools because there’s not enough money and they have to pay to rebuild all their schools at once and feels Orem would be in exactly that same situation. Ms. Hyatt concluded by saying that she feels they are not the ones that need to pull away from Alpine School District, that they need to move forward and be thoughtful about how this change could take place and not strip themselves of their rights as Orem citizens. Scott Price, an Orem resident, stated he has four children who are active in Orem schools. He stated everyone is talking about the details and statistics but he feels it is about the principle of the matter. Orem controls its water and Orem controls its power, and those are their most valuable physical resources. But nothing is more valuable of a resource than our children, and so we would not delegate the responsibility for caring for them and teaching them to people in American Fork. As nice as they may be, their interests are in American Fork. WHe asked the Council, who is going to know better how to teach your children and who to vote for that’s going to educate your children better than the parents themselves. He stated that he felt an Orem-only district could handle any of the problems mentioned. He concluded by stating they do have a bone to pick with Alpine School District and there are things they want to get back at them for, referring to the two years of restrictions due to the pandemic. Pat Mossbacker teaches and is the father of six Orem school students. He believes that the whole premise of the split is flawed. He feels we are part of a community. By the reasoning that Orem is somehow being wronged financially, other cities should be mad they’re ‘subsidizing’ our Orem students. He said that it is a narrow perspective pitting his kids against other kids, and it is a false financial hope that it will end up hurting the Orem kids. He stated the study says teachers are so important that they should be paid ten percent more. He stated that all of us are saying the rosy projections are not accurate; we’re not just afraid of change. He indicated he personally voted for most of the members on the Council, and they made promises to preserve neighborhoods and stand up to special interests, and feels they’ve largely kept those promises. He stated the City Council and the Planning Commission specifically preserved a residential zone down the hill from his home. He thanked them but stated it has been such a gut punch with this huge proposal and study that were never mentioned in their campaigns, have been rushed through that’s a special interest, and that is going to hurt Orem neighborhoods, the divisive campaign will undermine their credibility and all of the good neighborhood things that he hopes they can accomplish for the rest of their terms. He asked the council to look at the numbers and see through the pie in the sky promises that are going to leave Orem kids holding the bag. He asked them to listen to the large majority of their constituents. He said that no one’s voice is being taken away if you vote no. If the public uproar against the proposal wasn’t real then they’ll easily be able to gather signatures and put it on the ballot next year. Mr. Mossbacker concluded by asking the City Council to use their elected judgment and vote against putting this divisive proposal on the ballot. Michelle Lee, an Orem resident, stated in the past few years alone her kids have been in schools in three different states; each year she has different experiences in different school districts. She indicated in each of the school districts she came from, each school district only represented one or two cities, and Alpine School District represents fourteen cities. She stated in her other three school districts, there are between four and twelve schools included in those districts, but Alpine has ninety-two schools. In those three districts in different states across the country, there were between 2,200 and 6,200 students; Alpine has 85,000 students, and that is way too big. She explained that she had a really strong voice in her other school districts and it was very easy to volunteer and speak to her school board members. They were all local to her city and she was able to be heard and her kids had access to wonderful specialty programs and they had a great local experience. To speak to the previous comment, she feels it’s not about pitting kids against kids in different parts of the district. Orem kids are losing programs, Orem kids don’t have the same access to programs that other parts of the district have and that is the problem. She feels kids need to have the same experience, not different experiences based on different zip codes they live in. She feels smaller is better and local is better, the research is very clear on that, she also knows a split is inevitable, according to Alpine School District, so why can’t we do it on our Orem’s terms. She stated the board members have indicated they have studied this out themselves so why are they so opposed to Orem City being able to study it out themselves. Sara Hacken mentioned she put 7,000 miles on her car visiting schools in the district, that’s because we have 92 schools in the district, that is too big. Ms. Lee concluded by stating, think how much more of a voice we’d have with seven school board members all from Orem. John Wayas , an Orem resident, stated he grew up attending Orem schools, and currently has children who attend Orem schools and participate in the Spanish dual immersion program. He indicated that currently through Alpine School District, Orem is able to provide four dual immersion programs. He explained that he also lived in Murray for five years and his oldest son started his school career there and he knows for a fact that they have a great district and good teachers but they are not able to provide the level of services that Orem is able to have through Alpine School District. He stated Murray has one dual immersion program and one gifted program. He continued, indicating they also had trouble keeping Murray kids in Murray schools and in just his neighborhood alone half the kids went to Murray schools, others went to neighboring districts because they had more services, more programs, and for that reason he is here to speak tonight. He understands this vote and this process is injecting a high level of uncertainty in his children’s education and there is no guarantee they will get the same level of services in an Orem district. He believes there is a chance, but it is very uncertain that it can be accomplished without a high level of funds and tax dollars coming into the city to make up the difference to keep those programs. Mr. Wayas concluded by saying that he would like certainty and this is injecting a high level of uncertainty into hundreds of children’s lives and encouraged the Council to vote no.

Greg Brough stated he has observed in past council meetings they all have begun with a prayer each time thanking God for that which they have and petitioning Him to bless the deliberation and decisions of our community leaders and to bless each of us to be kind and civil to one another. He has been saddened to observe in the media and in some of the pronouncements of speakers before this body, the anger and disruption of civility that should prevail and the efforts of some who would take away freedom of choice, freedom of speech, and instead proffer untruths and half-truths in trying to sway public opinion. The study that was commissioned has helped to uncover many of the truths that have been hidden in the past. We may be looking beyond the mark tonight. A wise governor once said, “Now it is not common that the voice of the people desires anything contrary to that which is right, but it is common for the lesser part of the people who desire that which is not right. Therefore, this shall you observe and make it your law to do your business by the voice of the people.” He stated they are voting tonight whether to give the voters of the city the right to determine their own destiny regarding the schooling of their children and grandchildren. Mr. Brough concluded by stating he hopes Council members will rise above the attempts to intimidate, threaten, quash and distribute and disrupt proceedings to let the voters decide. Orem voters are the ones who know what their children and grandchildren need and what they are or are not receiving. They are the ones who can determine the future of education in our community, they also the ones who will incur the costs of benefits through the payment of property taxes. I plead with you to let the people of Orem decide. Please allow Orem voters to decide whether to stay or split from Alpine School District. Virgina Sokolowski stated it is interesting to see how good people can have such diversity of opinion. She voiced her concern as she has watched things happen in the Orem City government this year and feels a few of the city officials are grouping together to promote a hidden agenda. Splitting Orem schools from Alpine School District is one of the agenda items that is being promoted and that concerns her a lot. She explained that the Orem City website says the city of Orem believes transparency to be one of the pillars of good governance. She feels you can’t have some of the council grouping together and discussions of agendas items be transparent, they can’t exist together. She said the projections made by Discovery Educations Consultants concerning the split, they really can’t promise that their projections will become reality, that taxes will rise a minimum amount or that classrooms will be smaller or that we will have money to seismically retrofit our schools and you’ve heard the figures on how much the taxes have increased with the Jordan and Canyons split. Ms. Sokolowski concluded stating she and many others feel like it’s not the right time to split. To her a City Council should come together and decide things as a group and if some members are grouping together she feels that is not how a City Council should work. Gwenna Terry indicated for the past two weeks she has been racking her brain for something to say that would make a difference in the decision process today. She came to the realization that nothing she says will impact the decision this evening but she also knew that she needed her voice to be heard. She does believe they need to have a smaller school district and she has believed that for several years. She has looked forward to this feasibility study and to further the discussion, however she has been disappointed in the information given in the study after reading it over several times and doing some fact checking. She has discovered several flaws in the data and it was disheartening when the questions she presented to be answered were not answered in the community meetings. Ms. Terry looks forward to this being put on the ballot, but until she has more information and concrete answers to her concerns an Orem school district is not going to be the answer and her vote will be no. Keith Wilson, an Orem resident, thanked the Council for the opportunity to address them. He stated he was asked if he was opposed to a split of any kind and he is not. He stated he believes there are many other Orem residents who would support an honest study that included neighboring communities and open engagement with Alpine School District. He mentioned that is not what he feels is being promoted, so although he is not opposed to any kind of split, he is adamantly opposed to an Orem only split. An Orem only district is clearly the most expensive option, it is also the most disruptive option, forcing boundary changes on every school in Orem. also leaves Orem schools weaker. He stated that the Orem only proposal is half finished, with way too many gaps and unanswered questions. He commented about how often they heard questions were outside the scope of the studyHe stated one problem with some of the numbers in the study is that Provo School District has been held up for comparison even as a model, Orem only district would be a little larger than Provo, 14,800 students to Provo’s 13,600, about 1,200 more students. They can say roughly the same size, but wouldn’t you expect the budgets for district services to be approximately the same but DEC’s proposed budget for Orem is $21.6 million while Provo’s budget is $41.4 million, not even remotely close. He commented that teachers are concerned about their salaries and benefits but they are also very concerned about the support they receive or won’t receive from the district. Mr. Wilson concluded by asking the council to please support the teachers and their children and vote against putting this on the ballot Chelcie Loutensock, an Orem resident, stated she’s found online coming through the schools through field trips and after school programs, content on transgender, racism, and Nazism. She found these online and has pulled things off websites. She explained that she went to a legislative session where they had a group that made a presentation about bringing mental health clinics into schools, which the legislation seemed to be in favor of. Upon further research she indicated surveys were misleading to this presentation. Ms. Loutensock concluded by stating children are the brightest light and are everything good in this world and they are supposed to protect them. Aaron Anderson, an Orem resident, stated he has four children in Orem schools. His first observation is that leaders should build consensus and this process has not been pursued in a way designed to build consensus. He feels they could build consensus in this community around the idea that if it should be split, it would be best to split it in half. He believes there would be a widespread agreement between all sides, that it makes more financial sense for Orem to pair with neighboring cities than try and go it alone. He stated that an Orem only school district will have a shrinking student population. He stated it may seem harmless and only fair to let this go to the ballot, but if you rush this to a vote and it passes, you’ll lose a seat at the table to create something far more sustainable and less burdensome to Orem taxpayers. He feels that by looking at the six options presented by DEC it seemed like the only way DEC could claim that Orem property taxes would not increase more than they would if we stayed in Alpine School District was by proposing a $25 million-dollar bond and this would barley be enough to do a patchwork fix of seismic issues but still leave us with old facilities. He continued stating the most likely way Orem will be able to affordably rebuild its old schools and retain excellent teachers is by staying in Alpine School District. Mr. Anderson concluded by asking the citizens of Orem to cite the same founding fathers who wisely knew that thirteen colonies as different as they were would be stronger together than they would be apart, what a mistake an area of judgment it would be if any of those thirteen colonies decided to go at it alone. He asked the Council to vote no.

Dennis Lisonbee stated he had children and now has grandchildren in Orem schools. He referred to a statement on the Alpine School Districts website. Some of the things that matter to him are: Creating schools where Orem children will be protected. Facilitate lower class sizes; Increase teacher pay. Mr. Lisonbee concluded by stating that smaller class sizes and higher teacher salaries will allow curriculum and programs to be implemented that will improve student text scores. Jennifer Young, an Orem resident and an educator, commented on the history of feasibility studies in the state of Utah within the last 16 to 18 years. She indicated why it was or was not feasible for them to part with Alpine School District. Ms. Young concluded saying that she hopes that Orem can learn from those mistakes of past districts, and thanked the Council for giving the people the opportunity for the first time to vote on it. Mayor Young thanked those that were present and those that the Council has heard from regarding this issue. He turned the time to the Council for their comments. Tom Macdonald stated he believes this is the most important vote that he will cast in his almost nine years on the City Council. He indicated he had taken this very seriously, reading the report, attending meetings, and he agreed with many of the ideas in the report whether they split from the Alpine School District or not. Specifically he looked at exploring the possibility of outsourcing various services. They all recognize the benefits of smaller class sizes and higher salaries for their teachers. He does not think that some things can be overlooked or ignored and they need to look at test scores. He agrees with issues that were brought out and many other things many citizens were concerned about using a newly formed, untested company, Discovery Education Consultants, because of the previously publicly stated bias of Dr. Paul McCarty. This study found what others have said - a split is feasible. We’ve known this for some time. His concern was the undefined costs and how all these miracle cures would take place. He explained that they have spent a lot of money studying this and they will still spend a lot of money putting this on a ballot if we choose to go that way. He voiced his appreciation to Mr. Mike Wankier who was the financial person with Discovery that took the time to talk to him and told him yes, taxes would be higher in a separate school district than staying with Alpine, but the exact amount of that increase could not be determined. He agrees with that because so many assumptions would have to be made it would be unreasonable to make all of those assumptions and then take a guess at which assumptions worked. He believes the total cost of the actual split and setup of the cost would be huge. He believes that it is unreasonable to expect the standalone Orem district to operate at less than their pro rata share of the Alpine School District. That being said, he continued to state if this vote were just to split from Alpine School District, he would vote ye,s but not as an Orem stand alone. He thinks it’s too small, however when he walked in and saw campaign managers and t-shirts, he knew that this was going through tonight. He said he feels it has already been decided. He stated he would not vote for a split if it raises taxes and this will. It would be unfair for businesses thinking about locating to Orem as well as those who are already here. It would also be hard for those on a limited income, who we like to talk about regularly in our meetings, and with all those who believe that governments should spend reasonably and responsibly. To move forward before we know how much those taxes will raise reminds him of something Nancy Pelosi said in 2010, “We’ll have to pass the bill so you can find out what’s in it.” Mr. Macdonald concluded saying that he does not plan to do that. Debby Lauret stated in the springtime Ada Wilson and Sara Hacken were very kind to help set up meetings with Rob Smith. She was able to look at everything for the Title I schools for which they have seven, with full-time equivalent teachers. She indicated she had read all 280 pages of the feasibility study and attended 2 of the 3 meetings that the city supported. She stated she is taking her responsibility very seriously. She loves the idea of local control; she does agree that those closest govern best, she loves the idea of smaller class sizes and paying teachers more. Her concerns are shared service agreements with special education and transportation. She indicated the city would only be able to be reimbursed for up to half a million dollars and if any other cost were to be incurred they would have to take out a loan. She explained they have parks and streets and people to pay so that was very concerning to her. She feels with inflation and going into a recession it can be nerve wracking not to mention the possibility of a 4-18% property tax increase. She has been told in meetings that they get an extra $1,075 dollars out of unrestricted general funds above the other students in Orem. The rest of Alpine School District, some of these are full time equivalents, and that is about $4,000 that follows the student and the weighted pupil that comes from our income tax. She thinks that splitting is something that we need to consider, but she would like it to be a Vineyard, Orem, Lindon, Pleasant Grove and maybe even American Fork district. She has enjoyed their meetings with Alpine School District, they are productive, meetings of common interests, they worked together, and she would like to see this again. She believes that Alpine is too big but she would like to see it done in a way that is either North and South or East and West. Mrs. Lauret concluded her hesitations are increased property tax, the upfront cost the city would have to pay, whether we can negotiate service agreements and whether this is a better discussion with a wider scope.

David Spencer stated this topic was covered in 2006, 2017 and 2022. He said that in 2005 Alpine School District had 54,737 students and today they have over 85,000 students and he feels that is too big. In November 2016 Alpine School District did a bond for $387 million, plus they did a $77million lease revenue bond. Out of that $464 million, Orem received $4 million for the roof at Timpanogos High. He then went through and broke down the amount of money that each location received. He indicated if they were to go back to 2006 the council would have paid $312 million into the capital debt fund to Alpine School District and received $189 million back. That is $123 million going out of Orem and into other cities. He does not feel it is a good return on their investment and they are losing a lot of money. He continued they still have 4 schools that are not seismic safe. His main concern is these are all Title I schools and Alpine School District has known about those schools not being safe for 16 years. He asked Ada Wilson and Sara Hacken as board members to fight for Orem. He stated property taxes are increasing because of the Alpine School District. He indicated he has not seen anything on his property tax bill statement about the $595 million bond because Alpine School District is preventing sticker shock. He stated he has been told it is not a good time to do the split because of inflation, but he has looked at his taxes from 2008 to 2012 and Alpine School Districts taxes went up. He spoke about bussing and how much it would cost and stated that he believes the money should stay in Orem. Mr. Spencer stated his family history includes those that fought for our freedoms and stated they have the right to choose as Americans and the right to vote.

LaNae Millett stated she has spoken with people in the Canyons and Jordan Districts and the reason it was two to three hard years is because people created that with their attitudes, their responses, and their treatment of each other. She spoke about her involvement in schools and the impact she has had with them. She commented on the feasibility study and her unbiased approach to this issue. She indicated she attended 3 different meetings where she discussed financials with others. She attended PTA meetings in Orem and helped the parents understand what Orem City Council was doing, and explained the process that they were following. She stated in order for Orem alone to vote on this they could not include other cities because then it would be a district wide vote and likely would not pass. She explained some of the things that she learned while looking over the feasibility study. She is concerned that Alpine School District knew about seismic issues since 2006, and she has tried to mention ways to fix the issue but has gotten nowhere because of lack of funds. She continued speaking about large class sizes with not enough teachers, and said that students are leaving to go outside the district for further education. She continued to discuss things that the Canyons District has done over the past 13 years. She said that the Canyons District did all of this without raising taxes, and an Orem district would be able to do many of the same things. Mrs. Millett concluded saying that an Orem district is financially feasible and would thrive, it will allow the children to have the educational opportunities and the funding they deserve. Terry Peterson discussed our founding fathers and the right Americans have to vote. He indicated State statutes require districts to take care of special needs children and so that would not be an issue. He spoke about his experience while being on the Alpine School Board and how the board is always deciding how they move money. He said that Alpine School District has 14 cities and 85,000 students, it is the largest school district in the state of Utah. He commented it was disturbing to him that in the last 20 years there has been over $130 million that has left Orem to build schools outside of Orem. He stated Orem has been the largest financial contributor to Alpine School District since it was founded over 100 years ago. He stated that the student population of Orem is not decreasing. He proposed the idea of merging Orem with 13 cities and compared the struggles of what that would be to the same struggles that Alpine School District has. He does not feel a bigger school district is always better, because it is just too big. He explained that our taxes are going to go up every year, but wouldn’t it be nice if we kept our taxes here in Orem. He stated they cannot go back and get the $130 million dollars back, all they can do now is say let’s make the best of today by taking care of the families in Orem and focusing on our children. Mr. Peterson concluded if Orem were to become their own district it would consist of over 15,000 kids and it would still be one of the biggest districts in the state of Utah. Jeff Lambson stated he believes that everyone wants what is best for their children and he thanked everyone for their time, efforts and concerns. He explained this is not about re-election to him, this is an irreversible decision that will have ramifications for generations and decades to come. He wanted everybody to know that the decision did not come easy for him. He commented in Steven R Covey’s book the Seven Habits of Highly Effective People, there is a story that teaches about a business with producers or workers who get things done and the managers who oversee the work that the producers are doing and they make sure that everything they need to keep producing and then there are the leaders who climb to the top of the tallest tree, survey the entire situation and sometimes they have to yell, “wrong jungle.” He stated he was talking with a good friend just the other day and he said he had started and ran a successful business, and sometimes you just have to take a leap of faith. They are talking about taking a leap but he said he does not know that he has complete faith like base jumpers. Before they jump, they make sure that they have a parachute, they’re made aware of the obstacles and they know which way the wind is blowing. In his opinion the council is in the wrong jungle, and this is not the best time to jump. He believes there needs to be a split, but this may not be the best time to do this and take this leap of faith. He spoke about inflation, too much risk, and not enough details to put this forward on the ballot. He wants everybody to take some more time to work together and come together in creating something amazing. He is concerned about teachers, the senior members of their community, and tax increases. Mr. Lambson concluded by voicing his concern of unsafe schools and would like the school board to make this a top priority in the upcoming budget. Mayor Young stated they all would like the same thing and that is for the best education possible for their children. They want their teachers to be paid fairly, they don’t want their taxes too high and the issue before them is that we have different visions of how they can get there. He stated some facts that he knows are true about test scores declining, class sizes are higher than the national average, and kids that live in Orem’s boundaries not attending Alpine School District. The Mayor stated he had tried to meet with Alpine School District, once when the study was completed and again before the meeting tonight and they either canceled or extended the meeting which made it impossible for them to meet. He feels Alpine School District wants to pass the largest bond in their 170 year old history, and they know that this will almost double the amount of debt that the taxpayers will be liable for. He stated Alpine School District is one of the main recipients of Orem’s tax money, 100% of what Orem pays in state income tax goes to education which includes Alpine School District. Mayor Young concluded he believes it does not make sense that Orem taxpayers are paying millions towards other schools and cities, he understands both points of view on this debate and he sees benefits to both.

Blydan Lounsack spoke about forming an Orem school district. As a former teacher he feels he brings a very unique experience. He believes that he has a good perspective as to why a smaller district is better

Cindy Neilson commented about the parking permit in the Springwater area or Orem. She stated that because the City Council and Mayor approved the apartments with insufficient parking that they follow up with making sure there is enough parking for their structure.

Lesli Havili spoke about licensing agreement that she does not believe should apply to her because she has family currently living in the home not renters. She would like to have the property late fee and the licensing fee waived. Mr. Davidson asked her to speak with Steven Downs outside of the council chambers to help resolve the issue.

Murry Low commented regarding The Greens apartments. He would like the students to not be able to live there because there are no rules, he said that the students at UVU do not live in a natural and safe environment. He is wondering if there is something that the city can do about the living situation. He would encourage them to find somebody to influence the situation. Scott Hendricks commented regarding the parking permit on Springwater. He feels the City Code does not require enough parking stalls for the number of residents. voiced his frustration in the current parking situation. He stated that most students are going to have vehicles and there is not enough parking for all of them. He would like developers to be required to provide more parking.

Karen Adamson introduced herself as an Orem city resident. She thanked the council for their courage in serving the city. Ms. Adamson, her husband, and her children have all attended schools withing the Alpine School District. She is concerned with the growth of Alpine School District. Her husband is a builder and she has witnessed the growth in the community and the challenges that are associated with it. She believes that we have the resources and leaders within Orem who can create collaboration and relationships with all of our neighbors while taking care of Orem residents. John Barrick commented about the Orem only district and compared years and dollar amounts that he has researched. He discussed topics about the Alpine School District and funds/revenues associated with financial statements.

Amy Carr introduced herself as an Orem resident and a patron/volunteer/employee at the Orem library for 20 years. She has been involved in the children’s departments in the library and has helped represent numerous community groups. She personally helped curate black history month picture books, helped with black history story time, and wrote black history story time podcast episodes in previous years. She voiced her confusion when she found out that the library was no longer celebrating and doing displays about black history month this year in October when she was going to be doing story time. She has reached out to the director of the library and has asked a few people and she cannot figure out where the directive had come from. Ms. Carr spoke about an experience with her African American daughter in the library in 2020 and 2021. She feels that due to the lack of the black history month display her daughter did not feel welcome coming in the meeting at that time. Mayor Young expressed his concern as to why her daughter would be fearful to come in to the meeting.

Blyden Loutenzock visited a city council meeting in Burbank, CA a few weeks ago. This has made him appreciate Orem's City Council and Mayor. He continued to discuss a letter he received from the Lt. Governor's office. He believes that the Stronger Together PIC is still ongoing in their efforts. He is asking the City Attorney what is the status of the case.

Martha Harrison is here to represent the cottage people. This is the Cottages of the Fields, just off Geneva Road. She wants to bring up the issues in this area. She claims that the development was not completed as originally submitted. She would like Orem City to put pressure on the development to complete the project. She was referred to Mr. Bench in Development Services.

Jordan Christensen is a Vineyard resident. He is here to discuss the pedestrian fatality on 400 South. He believes that this will happen again if the City of Orem and Vineyard don't take immediate action. Mayor Young explained that he has spoken with the Vineyard Mayor and that this area is being discussed.

Tyler Haroldsen is a Vineyard resident. He is here to discuss the same pedestrian fatality as well as a student who was injured over a year ago. He is asking the City to do something and make this safer. He would like to see improvements to the Master Plan to protect pedestrians.

John Barrick is here to speak about election interference. He read parts of the letter from the Lt. Governor's Office. He says that Stronger Together PIC has dissolved but they sent 6 letters prior to this dissolution. He is saying the Stronger Orem is the same PIC as Stronger Together. He wants the City Attorney to look into this matter.

Jon Duffi came to speak about ADU's (accessory dwelling units). He presented the Orem City Code concerning ADU's. He has questions about ADU's and the need to have a shared wall that connects the units. He would like the city to allow ADU's that are separate standing units.

David Richardson lives in Orem and has come to discuss a problem with the City Council. He is noticing that his neighborhood has excessive street parking. He pointed out that some loopholes that he believes are in the city code concerning street parking. He would like the City to look into updating the code.

Bill Stay has multiple homes in Orem. He is concerned about the homes in his neighborhood that are a blight to the City and that City code is not enforced. He understands the process for compliance and he believes that more staff is needed in the Neighborhood Improvement Team.

Ashlee Taylor is the executive director of The Refuge Utah. This month is Domestic Violence Awareness month. She is here to speak about the programs that are available at the Refuge. She encouraged everyone to work together to make our community and homes safer and happier.

Jessica Ballard lives near Trader Joe's and she is frustrated with the traffic that comes into her neighborhood thinking that they can get to the mall. She would like the City to look into ways to discourage drivers from coming into the neighborhood looking to go to the mall.

Debbie Lamb lives near Trader Joe's and she has concerns about the stop signs that are not visible. She would also like to have additional signs that let drivers know that there is no mall access through their neighborhoods. She is also concerned about the high amount of illegal rentals in the neighborhood. She would like to see code enforcement enforce the rules.
